# Distribution Shift {#sec-shift}

Every earlier chapter assumed that the target distribution $p$ stands still and that the only
gap between training and deployment is how $q$ was drawn from it. Deployment does not stand
still: users change, sensors drift, prices move. When the world itself moves, the training data
describes a distribution that no longer exists. This chapter names the kinds of shift by which
part of $p$ changes, shows which kinds can be detected without labels, and says which of the
levers can repair each kind.

## The problem

A model is trained on data from one period and used in the next. Has the distribution changed?
If so, in a way that matters to the model, in a way that can be corrected, or only in a way that
new labels can reveal?

## Assumptions

1. **Shift happens between periods, not within them.** Data within a period is i.i.d.; gradual
   drift is approximated by comparing a recent window with a reference window.
2. **One kind of shift at a time.** Real shifts mix kinds, and the taxonomy below describes the
   pure cases.
3. **Input-only tests see only inputs.** A test that compares the inputs of two periods can
   detect a change in $p(x)$ and nothing else. Detecting anything else requires labels.

## Derivation or demonstration

**A taxonomy by which factor changes.** Moreno-Torres et al. unify the terms used across the
literature [@morenotorres2012unifying, Definitions 1–4]. *Dataset shift* is any difference
between the joint training and test distributions. Three special cases are distinguished by
which factor of the joint changes:

- **covariate shift** "appears only in X→Y problems", where inputs cause the label: $p(y \mid x)$
  is unchanged and $p(x)$ changes;
- **prior probability shift** "appears only in Y→X problems", where the label causes the
  inputs: $p(x \mid y)$ is unchanged and $p(y)$ changes;
- **concept shift**: the conditional changes ($p(y \mid x)$ in X→Y problems, $p(x \mid y)$ in Y→X
  problems) while the other factor does not.

The distinction is causal: which factor stays fixed depends on the direction of cause. It
decides the remedy. Under covariate shift, importance weighting by $p(x)/q(x)$ re-targets the
risk ([Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling)). Under prior shift,
the prior-shift correction re-targets the posterior, and EM estimates the new prior from
unlabeled data. Under concept shift, no reweighting of old examples can help: the old labels
answer a question that is no longer asked.

**Detecting shift.** A classifier two-sample test "pair[s] the n examples in $S_P$ with a
positive label, and … the m examples in $S_Q$ with a negative label"; if the two samples come
from the same distribution, "the classification accuracy of a binary classifier on a held-out
subset … should remain near chance-level" [@lopezpaz2016revisiting, abstract]. The testbed's
version fits a logistic regression on half of each sample. It then tests whether the classifier's
scores on the held-out halves separate the two samples, using a one-sided Mann–Whitney U test.
That test is valid when there is no shift, because the held-out scores are then exchangeable.
Over 400 no-shift seeds its p-values were uniform
(`tests/test_shift_detection.py::test_classifier_two_sample_test_is_calibrated_under_no_shift`).
For comparison, a simpler test runs a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on each feature and corrects
for the three tests.

On T1, with 500 examples in each sample and 200 seeds:

- **no shift:** the two tests rejected at rates {{< var ch10.none_c2st >}} and
  {{< var ch10.none_ks >}}, at a level of 0.05;
- **covariate shift:** moving the mean of $z_1$ by 0.1 standard deviations was detected
  {{< var ch10.cov01_c2st >}} of the time by the classifier test; by 0.3 standard deviations,
  {{< var ch10.cov03_c2st >}} and {{< var ch10.cov03_ks >}};
- **prior shift** from a class share of 0.5 to 0.3 changes $p(x)$, because $p(x)$ is a mixture of
  the classes: detected {{< var ch10.prior_c2st >}} and {{< var ch10.prior_ks >}} of the time;
- **concept shift**, the same inputs labeled by a different rule: {{< var ch10.concept_c2st >}}
  and {{< var ch10.concept_ks >}}, no more than with no shift. A labeled check, the deployed
  model's accuracy on 500 labeled new examples, detected the concept shift
  {{< var ch10.concept_labeled >}} of the time, and fired {{< var ch10.none_labeled >}} of the time
  with no shift
  (`tests/test_shift_detection.py::test_input_tests_detect_covariate_and_prior_shift_not_concept_shift`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: you can detect only what you observe"}
A test that compares inputs can detect any change in $p(x)$: covariate shift, and prior shift
whenever the classes differ in their inputs. Its power grows with the size of the shift and
the size of the samples. Concept shift leaves $p(x)$ unchanged, so no input-only test can see
it; only labels from the new period can.
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/shift-detection.md >}}

**Evidence that shift is common.** Recht et al. built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet
following the original collection procedures. The paper reports "accuracy drops of 3% – 15% on
CIFAR-10 and 11% – 14% on ImageNet" across a broad range of models. It attributes them not to
test-set reuse ("adaptivity") but to "the models' inability to generalize to slightly 'harder'
images than those found in the original test sets" [@recht2019imagenet, abstract]. This is one
study, of two image benchmarks, as of its 2019 publication. It shows that even a careful
replication of a data-generating process produces a shift large enough to matter.

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
`scipy.stats.ks_2samp` compares one feature between two samples; with many features, correct
for the number of tests. A classifier two-sample test needs only a classifier and a held-out
half. Monitor labeled performance wherever labels arrive, however late: input monitoring
cannot see concept shift.
:::

## What it does to the learned model

Shift does not change the model. It changes what the model's fixed decisions are worth. Under
covariate shift the model is right where it was right, but it is now asked more often where it
saw few examples. Under prior shift its probabilities are miscalibrated by a factor that can be
estimated and removed. Under concept shift it is confidently wrong in a way that its inputs do
not reveal.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: rejection rate of a classifier two-sample test and of per-feature Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (500 examples per sample, level 0.05, 200 seeds) as the mean of one feature shifts. Panel B: the same tests, and a labeled accuracy check, under no shift, prior shift and concept shift. Shifts in the inputs are detectable from inputs; concept shift is visible only through labels.](../images/distribution_shift.png){#fig-distribution-shift}

@fig-distribution-shift shows the detection results. The failures:

- **Watching inputs, missing concepts.** A dashboard of feature distributions stays green
  while the rule linking features to outcomes changes (panel B).
- **Small shifts, small samples.** At 0.1 standard deviations, 500 examples per window
  detected the shift in about one seed in ten (panel A).
- **Detected but harmless, or undetected but harmful.** A test answers whether $p(x)$ changed,
  not whether the model got worse. A shift in a feature the model ignores raises an alarm; a
  shift concentrated where the model is weak may not.
- **The wrong correction.** Applying a prior-shift correction to a covariate shift, or
  importance weights to a concept shift, corrects a factor that did not change.

## What the toy cannot show

T1's shifts are clean: one factor changes, by a known amount, at a known time. Real shifts mix
kinds, drift gradually, and arrive with labels that are late, sparse or biased. The
demonstrations show what each test can see in principle, not what it will catch in a given
monitoring setup.
